TASK: The machinist was freeing a seized clamping lever on the vertical mill at the start of a setup. The task was underway because the lever had to be released before the fixture could be changed for the next job. Stage of the task: setup or preparation. Method in effect: SW-612 Vertical Mill Fixture Changeover. The task was not being performed as written. The difference from the written method was as follows: the written method says a seized lever is to be reported to maintenance rather than freed by hand, but the job was due to run that shift so it was pulled by hand first. Equipment involved: Vertical mill VM-07, fixture clamping lever. Equipment state at the time: de-energized and at rest or stopped. Equipment condition: The clamping lever has been stiff for several weeks and is on the maintenance backlog. PPE in use: Safety glasses and general purpose gloves. This matched the PPE specified for the task.

SEQUENCE: Immediately before the event: standing square to the mill with the right hand on the clamping lever at about shoulder height and the left hand braced on the machine table. At the moment of the event: a hard pull was applied to the lever, the lever gave suddenly and the right arm travelled back and up past shoulder height, at which point a sharp pain was felt in the front of the right shoulder. Immediately after the event: the machinist let go of the lever, stepped back from the mill holding the right arm against the body, and called the team lead from the next machine. The prior condition relates to a previous work-related case at this site. Change in the condition: The previously repaired right shoulder had full range of motion and no symptoms before this. After the lever gave, the arm could not be raised above shoulder height and the pain has been constant since.

MECHANISM: Load or force involved: a hard pull on a lever that had seized, estimated at around 40 pounds of force. The load moved the hand was at about shoulder height throughout and travelled up past it as the lever gave. Body position during the movement: the right arm was extended forward at shoulder height with the body square to the machine, and the arm travelled back and up when the resistance released. Assist device: A lever extension bar is kept at the machine but was not used because the lever was expected to free with hand force. This was a push, pull or carry rather than a lift. Point of contact and direction of force: the front of the right shoulder, with the force directed backward and upward as the resistance released suddenly.

CONDITIONS: Difference from a normal run of this task: The lever had been stiff for weeks but gave suddenly on this occasion rather than freeing gradually. Conditions at the point of injury: nothing notable about the environment. Timing: About 30 minutes into an 8 hour shift and roughly 3 minutes into the setup. The machinist had performed this task before. A known hazard, prior near miss, open action or risk assessment covers this task. Detail: The stiff clamping lever on VM-07 has been on the maintenance backlog for about six weeks and a work order is open. No guard, interlock, barrier or control was bypassed, missing, defeated or ineffective. Stop-work opportunity: The lever could have been reported to maintenance as the written method requires, but the job was due to run that shift and the wait was expected to be long.

IMMEDIATE ACTIONS: First aid at the scene: A cold pack was applied to the front of the right shoulder in the first aid room for about 15 minutes. This was given by a trained first aid responder. Notification: The team lead was told within about a minute and EHS within twenty minutes. Scene and equipment: The mill was left as it was and tagged out until maintenance had looked at the lever. Work at the location stopped. The machinist was sent to an offsite occupational clinic for evaluation.
